# AI collaboration

**Every line of this repository was generated by an AI assistant. None of it has
been rewritten by hand.** All 45 commits carry an `Assisted-by: Claude Code`
trailer, which is an accurate statement rather than a courtesy.

This document is the considered account of how that worked, what it was good at,
and — at greater length, because it is the more useful half — where it failed
and what those failures had in common.

The raw record is [`notes/ai-log.md`](notes/ai-log.md): 1,900-odd lines appended
as work happened and never tidied afterwards, including the wrong turns and the
rejected output. This file is the summary. Where they disagree, the log is what
actually happened.

- Tool: **Claude Code (Opus 5)**
- Scope: ten slices, from an empty directory to a deployed system
- Result: 473 tests, applied to a real Kubernetes cluster and signed into

---

## The arrangement

Work arrived as **slice briefs** written by a reviewer — a paragraph or two of
intent, constraints, and things not to do. Not tickets, and not specifications:
statements of what the slice was for, usually with one or two things named as
already decided.

Three rules made the difference, and all three are about what happens *before*
code:

**1. Questions before building.** Several briefs ended with "tell me your
approach and wait for my answer." Those pauses produced the two best decisions
in the project. The authentication slice asked how 376 tests would keep running
without a live Keycloak; the answer — mint tokens from a test-generated key and
mock *only* the JWKS fetch, so signature, issuer, audience, expiry and key
selection all run for real — is better than either option the brief offered. The
deployment slice asked about frontend runtime configuration; the answer
deviated from the approach the brief suggested, with reasons, and the deviation
was approved.

Neither would have surfaced from building first and explaining afterwards.

**2. Decisions get written down where the next reader trips over them.**
[`DECISIONS.md`](DECISIONS.md) records why the code looks as it does;
[`SCOPE.md`](SCOPE.md) records what is deliberately absent. Both exist because
of a specific failure mode: settled questions kept being re-opened several
slices later, by an assistant with no memory of having settled them.

**3. Scope is refused explicitly, not silently.** The reviewer rejected the same
feature — a ladder of sanctions applied to a person rather than to something
they wrote — three times, under three different names. It is now named as one
feature in SCOPE.md so the fourth variant does not arrive looking new.

---

## What worked

**Consistency at a scale that is hard to hold by hand.** Conventions declared in
slice one still hold in slice ten: SQL appears only in `*.repository.ts`,
permission rules only in `src/policy/`, one error envelope produced by one
middleware, counts derived rather than stored. Deviation was easy to catch
because the rules were written down and checked against.

**The seam paid off exactly as designed.** Authentication was deferred to slice
nine but authorization was enforced from slice one, behind a single function.
When Keycloak arrived, that function's body changed and nothing else did:
nothing in `src/policy/` moved, no service learned what a token is, no handler
gained a null check. The 220 existing route tests changed in two mechanical ways
— which repository resolves identity, and a header on each call — and not one
changed what it asserts.

**Explaining the reasoning in the code.** The comments say why, not what,
because "why" is the thing that is expensive to reconstruct. Several of them are
the only reason a later slice did not undo an earlier decision.

**Volume of careful work.** 473 tests, most asserting a specific failure mode
rather than a happy path, is more than would have been written by hand in the
same time.

---

## Where it failed

Six real defects reached a running system. Grouped by what would have caught
them, because the grouping is the finding.

### Nothing in the test suite could have caught three of them

| Defect | Where it lived |
|---|---|
| `postLogoutRedirectUris` — a client field Keycloak does not have | Keycloak realm JSON |
| `${env.WEB_ORIGIN}` — substitution the realm importer does not do | Keycloak realm JSON |
| `redirectUris` naming only `localhost:4200` | Keycloak realm JSON |

All three are **claims about another system's schema**, and the first two are
the same mistake made twice — the second while fixing the consequences of the
first. Both were confident inventions that read correctly to anyone who knows
OpenID Connect but not Keycloak specifically. Neither was a typo.

They also fail identically and unhelpfully: the importer rejects the **entire
file** rather than the bad field, so Keycloak will not start, so the container
restart-loops, and the only thing the orchestrator shows is a healthcheck
reporting `Connection refused` — a message containing no occurrence of "realm",
"import" or "client". The sentence naming the field is thirty lines up in
`docker logs` and nowhere else.

Throughout all of it the suite was green, and it was not wrong to be. The defect
was in a JSON document no test loads, consumed by a program no test runs,
validated by a schema written in Java.

**The lesson, now a rule:** a claim about another system's schema is checked
against that system's documentation before it reaches a file — and so is the
*fix* for a configuration problem, since that is also configuration. The trigger
is writing a key into a file some other program will parse: a realm import, a
compose file, a Kubernetes manifest, an nginx directive. In application code a
wrong name is a compile error in seconds. In these it is silent until something
will not start.

### Two more needed a browser

| Defect | Why the suite missed it |
|---|---|
| The authorization code redeemed twice, so a successful sign-in immediately reported failure | Angular's component lifecycle reacting to a signal the shell's template gates on |
| A circular dependency between the session service and the interceptor that injects it, so the **first** page load always failed | One spec provided the service without the interceptor; the other provided the interceptor with a stubbed service |

The second is the more instructive. Two specs, both passing, and the bug lived
precisely in the relationship between the things they each mocked. That is a
structural gap, not an oversight: mocking one side of a pair is how a pair goes
untested. It is now covered by a spec that stands both up together, and I
confirmed it fails against the old code before fixing it.

Both were found by a human opening the application. Neither was reachable by any
test that existed, and the second made every first page load fail — the single
most visible defect in the project, invisible to 460 passing tests.

### One was found by re-reading

The Kubernetes init container that holds the API back until the database is
ready waited for the `schema_migrations` **table to exist**. That is correct
exactly once — on a first install. On every deploy after, the table is already
there, so a release adding migration 13 would start the API against schema 12
and serve queries for columns that do not exist.

It reviewed well and it ran correctly the only time it had ever run. The bug was
reachable solely on the *second* deployment of a system that had never had a
first. Caught while answering a question about migrations, by nothing else.

---

## What the reviewer caught that the assistant did not

Worth listing separately, because these are not bugs — they are judgement, and
they are where the collaboration earned its keep.

- **Scope creep dressed as a recommendation.** A handoff proposed account
  deactivation as "the most valuable slice left", invented a question about what
  it should mean to the identity provider, and parked three candidate answers —
  for a feature already refused twice. Adjacency to what was just built is not
  scope, and it is exactly the kind of proposal that gets made without checking.
- **Re-opening a settled question.** Whether clearing `external_id` on account
  deletion was correct had been decided and recorded; it was raised again as
  though open.
- **Committed secret values.** Development credentials in a Kubernetes Secret's
  `stringData`, with a comment explaining why it was fine. The reviewer's point
  stands: a manifest is read as a statement of approach, and a reviewer registers
  real-looking values before they read the comment.
- **A capability described in three files that does not exist.** Documentation
  said a reviewer could "promote a regular user to admin". Nothing in this
  application promotes anybody. The phrase was carried from a conversational
  aside into three documents without being checked against the code — the same
  failure as the realm files, in prose.

---

## What changed in how the work was done

**Running it became a step, not a flourish.** Every slice after the first realm
failure ends with the thing actually running: containers up, the flow driven end
to end, manifests applied to a real cluster. That found five of the six defects
above. Nothing else would have.

**"Verified" became a narrower word.** The authentication slice was reported as
"verified against a live Keycloak, 35 checks" — true, and much narrower than it
sounded. It verified the protocol, not the application, and two browser-only
bugs were sitting in the part it did not reach. Claims now say what was
exercised and what was not.

**Gaps are named rather than quietly left.** A redeploy that adds a migration
while replicas are running is still untested; both branches of the init
container have been run in isolation, the sequence has not. That is written in
the handoff and in `k8s/README.md` rather than omitted.

---

## Honest limits

- **The screens have never been audited by a human** for layout, keyboard focus
  order, narrow viewports, or the dark scheme as an explicit choice. Every
  handoff since slice five has said so. Both browser-only defects came from this
  area, which suggests the debt is where the remaining defects are.
- **The French interface is complete and unexamined.** Three tests prove the
  catalogue has no gaps; nothing has checked whether the longer wording fits the
  controls.
- **AI-written tests can share the author's blind spot.** The circular-dependency
  bug is the proof: the same assistant wrote both specs and mocked the other side
  in each. Tests written by the thing being tested do not catch what it did not
  think of.
- **This is one long collaboration, not a demonstration of autonomy.** The
  reviewer set scope, refused features, chose between approaches, and caught the
  four judgement failures above. The assistant did the building and most of the
  verifying. Attributing the result entirely to either would be inaccurate.
